title: Fortinet Enterprise Networking & Security — 50-question graded examination

questions.stem: A FortiGate SNAT session changes source port 4500. The original port is below 5117. What should be checked first?

options.label: A
options.text: The port is below the documented preservation range, so normal allocation may translate it.
options.feedback: The preservation range begins at 5117; port 4500 can be translated normally.

options.label: B
options.text: A policy route rewrites UDP source ports before NAT under that NAT rule.
options.feedback: Policy routes select paths and do not generally rewrite transport ports.

options.label: C
options.text: The service object converts IKE traffic from UDP to TCP in the observed tuple.
options.feedback: A service object matches traffic; it does not convert UDP into TCP.

options.label: D
options.text: Central SNAT disables reverse mapping for all UDP sessions for this source port.
options.feedback: SNAT maintains a reverse session mapping for translated tuples.

questions.stem: Two sessions request the same preserved source port. One keeps it and the other changes. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: Port preservation applies only to the first packet of every UDP flow in the observed tuple.
options.feedback: The choice is made for the session and then tracked for later packets.

options.label: B
options.text: The tuple was already in use, so the second session needed another available port.
options.feedback: Preservation is conditional on tuple availability; collisions require another port.

options.label: C
options.text: The second session bypassed central SNAT after policy lookup for this source port.
options.feedback: An existing session does not make later traffic bypass the NAT rule base.

options.label: D
options.text: The remote server selected the translated client source port before a new flow.
options.feedback: The remote server normally does not choose FortiGate's SNAT port.

questions.stem: An existing flow keeps its old translated port after port-preserve is enabled. What is the best test?

options.label: A
options.text: Restart every HA member before testing the same traffic again for this source port.
options.feedback: A cluster restart is disproportionate and does not isolate the decision.

options.label: B
options.text: Change the destination to force an unrelated SNAT rule before a new flow.
options.feedback: Changing destination can change rule matching and confound the test.

options.label: C
options.text: Disable session helpers so the existing tuple is re-evaluated with the same destination.
options.feedback: Helpers do not cause an established NAT tuple to be recalculated.

options.label: D
options.text: Clear only the test session, create a new flow, and inspect its tuple.
options.feedback: Established sessions retain their translation; a new session tests the setting.

questions.stem: A low source port must map deterministically. What constraint must be checked?

options.label: A
options.text: Use ICMP with a port field and an interface-address pool before a new flow.
options.feedback: ICMP has no TCP/UDP-style port, and interface pools do not meet this mapping case.

options.label: B
options.text: Configure policy NAT even though central NAT is active with the same destination.
options.feedback: When central NAT is active, central-snat-map controls SNAT.

options.label: C
options.text: Use a supported port protocol and an overload pool with valid explicit mapping.
options.feedback: Explicit mapping has protocol/pool limits and maps source to translated ranges.

options.label: D
options.text: Assume any source port can be preserved without collision checks for this session.
options.feedback: NAT still requires a unique reverse mapping for each session.

questions.stem: An ADOM revision was restored, but the managed FortiGate still has the newer package. What completes rollback?

options.label: A
options.text: Restore the same ADOM snapshot repeatedly until the device reboots.
options.feedback: Repeated restore does not replace the missing installation step.

options.label: B
options.text: Lock the revision and assume the running device updates automatically.
options.feedback: A retention lock protects a snapshot but does not deploy it.

options.label: C
options.text: Import the device configuration as needed, then install the intended package.
options.feedback: ADOM restore changes the database; import and install align device state.

options.label: D
options.text: Delete the current package and wait for the snapshot to push itself.
options.feedback: Deleting the package removes management state instead of safely installing it.

questions.stem: Why lock a known-good ADOM revision before a migration?

options.label: A
options.text: To prevent administrators from viewing its revision diff in the selected ADOM.
options.feedback: The revision remains inspectable; locking is a retention control.

options.label: B
options.text: To prevent automatic retention cleanup from deleting the rollback snapshot.
options.feedback: The lock protects the revision from configured auto-deletion.

options.label: C
options.text: To make the snapshot apply to devices without an install operation.
options.feedback: A snapshot does not deploy itself to managed devices.

options.label: D
options.text: To convert it into a FortiGate running-config revision for the managed device.
options.feedback: ADOM and device configuration revisions are different objects.

questions.stem: Before restoring an ADOM snapshot, how can an engineer inspect its likely effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare the FortiGate session table with the SNAT tuple.
options.feedback: Session tables show traffic state, not ADOM object history.

options.label: B
options.text: Run an install and infer the differences from the result.
options.feedback: An install result is not a pre-restore comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: Delete the snapshot and inspect the current object database.
options.feedback: Deleting the baseline destroys the comparison point.

options.label: D
options.text: View Revision Diff against the current ADOM database.
options.feedback: Revision Diff previews database differences before restoring.

questions.stem: A device configuration revision is reverted, but the policy package is unchanged. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: FortiManager never stores managed-device configuration revisions after the restore before package install.
options.feedback: Managed-device revisions exist but differ from ADOM snapshots.

options.label: B
options.text: Device-config revert does not restore the ADOM package or other modules.
options.feedback: The revert scope is device configuration; package alignment is separate.

options.label: C
options.text: A device reboot regenerates the ADOM package automatically in the revision diff.
options.feedback: A reboot does not guarantee package synchronization.

options.label: D
options.text: Revision restore changes the FortiAnalyzer analytics database for that rollback point.
options.feedback: FortiAnalyzer database rebuilds are unrelated to FortiManager revisions.

questions.stem: A FortiAnalyzer fetch session says Done, but fetched logs are absent from reports. What next?

options.label: A
options.text: Check client indexing and ADOM/database rebuild progress.
options.feedback: Transfer completion precedes indexing; reports wait for the rebuild.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the server to retransmit because Done means no transfer occurred.
options.feedback: Done indicates transfer completion, not that the transfer failed.

options.label: C
options.text: Assume the server deleted the client's analytics database.
options.feedback: The workflow does not automatically delete the client's database.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable OFTP encryption on the syslog listener.
options.feedback: OFTP transport security is separate from post-fetch indexing.

questions.stem: When should the fetch client synchronize device and ADOM data with the server?

options.label: A
options.text: Only after every scheduled report succeeds within that ADOM.
options.feedback: Report generation occurs after the data becomes available.

options.label: B
options.text: On first use of a profile or after device/ADOM changes.
options.feedback: The guide calls for sync on first use and relevant inventory changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Only when the analyzers run different firmware versions for the same analyzer pair.
options.feedback: Log fetching requires same firmware, not different versions.

options.label: D
options.text: Every time a query runs against already indexed data.
options.feedback: Queries against indexed logs do not require a new fetch sync.

questions.stem: What firmware condition applies to a FortiAnalyzer fetch pair?

options.label: A
options.text: The client and server must run the same firmware.
options.feedback: Same-firmware compatibility is an explicit log-fetch requirement.

options.label: B
options.text: The client must always be newer than the server.
options.feedback: A newer client is not the stated prerequisite.

options.label: C
options.text: The server must be cloud-hosted and the client on-premises.
options.feedback: Cloud hosting is not required for log fetching.

options.label: D
options.text: Both appliances must use different ADOM names for the same device.
options.feedback: Device/ADOM mappings must be synchronized, not deliberately inconsistent.

questions.stem: Two analysts request different historical intervals from the same analyzer pair. What should they plan for?

options.label: A
options.text: Requests automatically merge into one unfiltered transfer on the fetching client.
options.feedback: Merging changes the requested time ranges and filters.

options.label: B
options.text: An analyzer can never act as both client and server for the requested interval.
options.feedback: An appliance can serve one peer and fetch from another peer.

options.label: C
options.text: A second request bypasses approval while the first is active after transfer completion.
options.feedback: Approval remains part of the workflow; concurrency does not bypass it.

options.label: D
options.text: Only one fetch session can run between that appliance pair at once.
options.feedback: The guide limits each pair to one concurrent fetch session.

questions.stem: An IP phone gets a data-VLAN lease despite an LLDP profile. What dependency is most likely missing?

options.label: A
options.text: FortiAnalyzer has not rebuilt its fetched-log database for the phone's VLAN on the voice path.
options.feedback: Log indexing does not affect Layer-2 VLAN selection.

options.label: B
options.text: An ADOM revision is locked against automatic deletion in the LLDP-MED profile before DHCP succeeds.
options.feedback: ADOM retention does not control switch-port behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: The phone's DHCP lease is shorter than the LLDP interval for the attached phone.
options.feedback: Lease timing cannot fix a missing VLAN advertisement or trunk membership.

options.label: D
options.text: The voice VLAN or profile is not correctly applied and carried on that port.
options.feedback: The phone needs the right TLV, profile assignment, and allowed VLAN path.

questions.stem: A capture shows LLDP-MED advertises DSCP 46. What does that prove?

options.label: A
options.text: The TLV advertises that value, not end-to-end QoS treatment.
options.feedback: The capture proves TLV content; downstream QoS needs separate verification.

options.label: B
options.text: Every upstream router now prioritizes voice packets automatically.
options.feedback: LLDP does not configure every upstream router's queues.

options.label: C
options.text: The phone accepted the VLAN and obtained a DHCP lease.
options.feedback: Advertisement does not prove endpoint acceptance or DHCP success.

options.label: D
options.text: Every trunk has the voice VLAN allowed and tagged.
options.feedback: The TLV does not prove VLAN membership on every trunk.

questions.stem: A standalone FortiSwitch receives a controller-managed LLDP profile example. What should be done?

options.label: A
options.text: Enable central SNAT so voice VLANs are advertised dynamically.
options.feedback: SNAT does not control LLDP advertisements.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the LLDP configuration hierarchy for the actual management mode.
options.feedback: Standalone and controller-managed switches use different configuration contexts.

options.label: C
options.text: Restore an ADOM revision to discover the wireless controller.
options.feedback: An ADOM revision does not make a standalone switch controller-managed.

options.label: D
options.text: Change FortiAnalyzer fetch roles to enable LLDP-MED in the LLDP-MED profile.
options.feedback: Log-fetch roles have no dependency on LLDP-MED.

questions.stem: The correct LLDP-MED TLV is visible, but the phone has no voice address. What next?

options.label: A
options.text: Assume DHCP is faulty because the TLV is correct.
options.feedback: The server may be fine if the phone never tags voice traffic.

options.label: B
options.text: Disable LLDP transmit to force a fresh DHCP request.
options.feedback: Disabling LLDP removes the advertisement instead of fixing later stages.

options.label: C
options.text: Verify phone acceptance, VLAN carriage, and the voice DHCP path.
options.feedback: The TLV proves advertisement only; tagging and DHCP remain separate stages.

options.label: D
options.text: Change FortiPAM approval tiers before retesting before DHCP succeeds.
options.feedback: PAM authorization does not affect voice VLAN DHCP.

questions.stem: An AP exceeds its station threshold. What does AP handoff try to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move a weak client to a nearby AP that can hear it adequately.
options.feedback: AP handoff selects weak stations only when a suitable neighbor exists.

options.label: B
options.text: Move every client to 5 GHz immediately on the neighboring AP for that station.
options.feedback: AP handoff differs from frequency handoff.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the SSID VLAN to the least-used network in this RF cell.
options.feedback: VLAN selection is unrelated to AP load balancing.

options.label: D
options.text: Disable roaming clients so they reconnect through the controller for the selected profile.
options.feedback: Roaming clients are excluded from the documented behavior.

questions.stem: Why might a dual-band client retry on 2.4 GHz with frequency handoff enabled?

options.label: A
options.text: Its measured 5 GHz RSSI may be below the configured threshold.
options.feedback: The controller uses band capability and 5 GHz signal strength to steer.

options.label: B
options.text: Frequency handoff requires every client to use WPA3 Enterprise for that station.
options.feedback: WPA3 is not a prerequisite for frequency handoff.

options.label: C
options.text: The controller cannot record RSSI for any 5 GHz client.
options.feedback: The controller records per-band RSSI for client decisions.

options.label: D
options.text: The AP handoff threshold selects the client's DHCP server in this RF cell.
options.feedback: AP handoff station count does not select a DHCP server.

questions.stem: An operator expects load balancing to move a client already roaming between APs. What limitation applies?

options.label: A
options.text: The feature works only when FortiAnalyzer fetching is enabled.
options.feedback: Log fetching is unrelated to wireless association steering.

options.label: B
options.text: The documented load-balancing feature is not applied to roaming clients.
options.feedback: The guide separates roaming behavior from load-balancing decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Roaming clients are always pinned to 2.4 GHz in this RF cell.
options.feedback: Band choice depends on capability and RSSI, not a universal pin.

options.label: D
options.text: The client needs an LLDP-MED voice VLAN before roaming.
options.feedback: LLDP-MED is a wired endpoint mechanism.

questions.stem: After aggressive handoff, retries rise while AP client counts fall. What evidence best diagnoses the cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Check only the total DHCP leases on the FortiGate.
options.feedback: DHCP totals do not show radio quality or association behavior.

options.label: B
options.text: Compare neighbor RSSI, channel utilization, retries, and association events.
options.feedback: These measurements show whether steering targets are usable and airtime is constrained.

options.label: C
options.text: Raise the station threshold without reviewing RF coverage.
options.feedback: Blind threshold changes may hide overload while retaining poor RF.

options.label: D
options.text: Disable all 5 GHz radios to remove retry counters.
options.feedback: Disabling 5 GHz defeats the design instead of diagnosing it.

questions.stem: A specific FortiNAC policy never wins while a broad profile sits above it. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: The specific policy loses because its name is shorter for the selected treatment.
options.feedback: Names do not determine precedence.

options.label: B
options.text: FortiNAC randomly chooses among matching policies before enforcement on that switch port.
options.feedback: The first match wins; selection is not random.

options.label: C
options.text: The earlier broad policy matches first and shadows the specific policy.
options.feedback: Policy evaluation is top-down first-match, so order controls treatment.

options.label: D
options.text: The access configuration overrides profile matching regardless of rank for this registered host.
options.feedback: The profile match selects the policy whose configuration supplies treatment.

questions.stem: A host is online in inventory but no Network Access Policy is evaluated. What prerequisite should be checked?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm the FortiPAM secret request is approved before enforcement on that switch port.
options.feedback: PAM approval is unrelated to NAC policy eligibility.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm FortiAnalyzer indexed historical host logs for this registered host in the ranked list.
options.feedback: Log indexing does not determine host registration.

options.label: C
options.text: Confirm the FortiGate SNAT port is above 5117 at evaluation time.
options.feedback: SNAT port preservation is unrelated to NAC policy evaluation.

options.label: D
options.text: Confirm registration and membership of the port in the Role-Based Access group.
options.feedback: Policy evaluation requires registered-host eligibility and the appropriate port group.

questions.stem: Which tool helps identify the ranked profile that matches a host before enforcement testing?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Policy Simulator, then inspect Policy Details on the host.
options.feedback: Policy Simulator tests criteria; Policy Details shows the assigned treatment.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the FortiAnalyzer fetch-session monitor and rebuild banner on that switch port.
options.feedback: Fetch monitoring tracks log transfer and indexing.

options.label: C
options.text: Use FortiPAM Approval List to inspect policy precedence for this registered host.
options.feedback: PAM approvals do not show NAC matching.

options.label: D
options.text: Use FortiGate session tuples to determine the NAC policy rank.
options.feedback: Session tuples show traffic translation, not policy selection.

questions.stem: FortiNAC selects the intended VLAN policy, but the switch port stays unchanged. What boundary is next?

options.label: A
options.text: Reorder every policy because selection cannot be correct if VLAN failed.
options.feedback: Changing order after a correct match can create a new error.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume registration is invalid despite the assigned policy.
options.feedback: The assigned policy shows the host entered evaluation.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the profile to match a broader catch-all policy.
options.feedback: A catch-all can shadow other policies and weaken specificity.

options.label: D
options.text: Inspect the network-access treatment and device enforcement result.
options.feedback: A correct match proves classification, not successful device actuation.

questions.stem: After upgrading FortiNAC-F to 7.4+, what should happen before disabling Legacy Proxy?

options.label: A
options.text: Delete all old proxy objects and rely on the global default.
options.feedback: Deleting objects first can break requests still using them.

options.label: B
options.text: Switch every device to Local RADIUS regardless of design on the RADIUS path.
options.feedback: Local and Proxy modes have different authentication/accounting behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: Validate Virtual Proxy objects and update each device, VDOM, or SSID binding.
options.feedback: Migration requires validating new objects and changing their references.

options.label: D
options.text: Disable accounting until the legacy tab disappears after the upgrade for the selected virtual server.
options.feedback: Disabling accounting hides rather than completes migration issues.

questions.stem: External RADIUS should handle 802.1X EAP while FortiNAC handles MAB locally. Which mode fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Use Local mode because it always forwards EAP externally.
options.feedback: Local mode terminates supported EAP locally.

options.label: B
options.text: Use Legacy Proxy for all new FortiNAC-F 7.6 configurations.
options.feedback: New configurations should use Virtual Servers, not the legacy view.

options.label: C
options.text: Use Local mode and expect it to provide accounting.
options.feedback: Local RADIUS does not provide accounting by itself.

options.label: D
options.text: Use Proxy mode with Proxy MAB Requests disabled.
options.feedback: Proxy forwards EAP; with Proxy MAB disabled, MAB can be local.

questions.stem: After migration, 802.1X works but accounting is absent. Which distinction matters?

options.label: A
options.text: A Virtual Proxy Server cannot handle authentication and accounting for the selected virtual server.
options.feedback: Virtual Proxy can handle both when configured for both.

options.label: B
options.text: The SSID must be moved into a central-SNAT policy before disabling legacy mode.
options.feedback: Central SNAT does not affect RADIUS accounting.

options.label: C
options.text: The shared secret determines whether Local RADIUS supports accounting on both HA nodes.
options.feedback: A shared secret secures RADIUS exchange but does not add Local accounting capability.

options.label: D
options.text: Local RADIUS does not provide accounting; configure the proxy accounting path.
options.feedback: Accounting is supported through the proxy path; Local does not supply it alone.

questions.stem: Which interface permissions should be verified for FortiNAC-F Local RADIUS?

options.label: A
options.text: Confirm radius-local and, when required, radius-acct access options.
options.feedback: Local RADIUS has its own access token; accounting uses a separate path.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable only legacy radius and remove all other access options.
options.feedback: Legacy proxy and Local RADIUS have distinct allowaccess requirements.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable OFTP and disable the RADIUS listener.
options.feedback: OFTP is unrelated to the FortiNAC RADIUS listener.

options.label: D
options.text: Set the FortiGate interface as a central-SNAT member.
options.feedback: Central-SNAT membership does not enable a RADIUS service.

questions.stem: A FortiAuthenticator request lacks NAS-IP-Address required by a policy. What should happen?

options.label: A
options.text: The policy matches because the user's password is valid in the ordered policy list.
options.feedback: Credential validity does not satisfy a missing selection attribute.

options.label: B
options.text: FortiAuthenticator infers NAS-IP from the username realm for this Access-Request.
options.feedback: Realm parsing does not substitute for the missing request field.

options.label: C
options.text: That policy fails its criteria and evaluation continues down the list.
options.feedback: Every configured request-attribute criterion must match.

options.label: D
options.text: The missing attribute forces all policies to be bypassed at policy selection.
options.feedback: The request may match a later/default policy rather than bypassing all policies.

questions.stem: EAP options are configured in a FortiAuthenticator policy, but the request is proxied. What is the boundary?

options.label: A
options.text: Those EAP settings apply to locally terminated EAP, not proxied sessions.
options.feedback: The guide distinguishes local EAP termination from proxy forwarding.

options.label: B
options.text: EAP settings always override the external server's response for this Access-Request.
options.feedback: The external server handles the proxied EAP session.

options.label: C
options.text: Proxy mode converts all EAP into local Password/OTP at policy selection.
options.feedback: Proxy does not automatically convert EAP to Password/OTP.

options.label: D
options.text: Policy order is ignored whenever EAP is enabled before identity lookup.
options.feedback: Policies remain ordered by request matching.

questions.stem: Two IPsec tunnels need different group outcomes from FortiAuthenticator. What discriminator is cleanest?

options.label: A
options.text: Use stable distinct request attributes such as NAS-IP-Address in ordered policies.
options.feedback: Distinct request attributes let each tunnel select the intended policy.

options.label: B
options.text: Give both tunnels identical NAS attributes and rely on policy names.
options.feedback: Policy names do not distinguish Access-Requests.

options.label: C
options.text: Put a no-criteria default policy at the top at policy selection.
options.feedback: A broad top policy captures requests before specific policies.

options.label: D
options.text: Change the certificate for every user login before identity lookup.
options.feedback: Certificate rotation is not normal tunnel-specific RADIUS selection.

questions.stem: How many request attributes can a FortiAuthenticator RADIUS policy use as criteria in the documented guide?

options.label: A
options.text: Any number, even if absent from the request before identity lookup.
options.feedback: Absent attributes cannot satisfy criteria.

options.label: B
options.text: Exactly one, always User-Name with the received attributes for that NAS client.
options.feedback: The documented maximum is not one and does not mandate User-Name alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Up to two, and the NAS must actually send them.
options.feedback: The guide documents up to two criteria, each of which must match.

options.label: D
options.text: None; policies match only identity sources in the ordered policy list.
options.feedback: Identity-source settings follow policy selection; they are not the only input.

questions.stem: An approver revokes a FortiPAM 1.9+ request after launch. What should occur?

options.label: A
options.text: Only future launches are blocked; the current session remains active after the approval decision.
options.feedback: The documented behavior includes termination of an already launched session.

options.label: B
options.text: The request is permanently approved and cannot be reviewed again for that requester.
options.feedback: The request resets and requires a new approval or denial.

options.label: C
options.text: The active secret session terminates and the request resets for a new decision.
options.feedback: Revoke Approval withdraws authorization and terminates the associated session.

options.label: D
options.text: All sessions for every FortiPAM user terminate in the session monitor for the active secret session.
options.feedback: Revocation is scoped to the request/session, not all users.

questions.stem: The revoke button is greyed out on an older FortiPAM deployment. What should be checked?

options.label: A
options.text: Assume the target server is unreachable because revocation requires SSH.
options.feedback: The issue may be approval-state semantics rather than target connectivity.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the version and whether a single-approver tier is already complete.
options.feedback: Older tier behavior can make a completed single-approver approval non-revocable.

options.label: C
options.text: Delete and recreate the secret in a new folder for that requester.
options.feedback: Deleting the secret is destructive and does not explain button state.

options.label: D
options.text: Disable all approval tiers so the request can be revoked.
options.feedback: Removing approval controls weakens authorization instead of fixing workflow.

questions.stem: How do you verify revocation cut off an active FortiPAM session?

options.label: A
options.text: Check only that the approval comment was saved in the session monitor.
options.feedback: A comment is audit context, not proof of session termination.

options.label: B
options.text: Check request reset and verify the session is gone from Active Sessions.
options.feedback: The operation affects both request state and active session state.

options.label: C
options.text: Check only the secret's password-change timestamp for the active secret session.
options.feedback: Password rotation is a different secret lifecycle event.

options.label: D
options.text: Check whether the target still resolves DNS in this request during revocation.
options.feedback: DNS reachability does not prove FortiPAM terminated the session.

questions.stem: Why might the approval request time differ between requester and approver?

options.label: A
options.text: FortiPAM stores all approvals in UTC and never displays local time.
options.feedback: The UI documents timezone display behavior, not UTC-only display.

options.label: B
options.text: The target server timezone exclusively determines approval display for the active secret session.
options.feedback: The target timezone does not exclusively determine the displayed time.

options.label: C
options.text: Approval times inherit the FortiGate firewall schedule in this request.
options.feedback: Firewall schedules are unrelated to PAM request time display.

options.label: D
options.text: The approver timezone is default unless requestor timezone display is enabled.
options.feedback: The dialog supports approver timezone and an option for requestor timezone.

questions.stem: A FortiSIEM rule groups by Source IP. Why can adding Destination Port reduce triggering?

options.label: A
options.text: Group By fields only label incidents after triggering for this rule mode.
options.feedback: Group By participates in threshold calculation, not just display.

options.label: B
options.text: Adding fields merges all groups into one larger count in the same group.
options.feedback: More grouping keys generally split groups rather than merge them.

options.label: C
options.text: The rule automatically switches from streaming to scheduled mode before incident creation.
options.feedback: Adding a field does not change execution mode.

options.label: D
options.text: Events split into more groups, so each group's count may fall below threshold.
options.feedback: Grouping defines aggregation buckets, so extra keys can fragment counts.

questions.stem: A Scheduled via SQL incident lacks trigger events. Which explanation is supported?

options.label: A
options.text: That ClickHouse rule mode does not expose trigger events in incidents.
options.feedback: The guide documents this mode limitation; absence alone is not parser proof.

options.label: B
options.text: The parser discarded all events before rule evaluation in the same group.
options.feedback: Parser behavior must be tested separately from rule mode.

options.label: C
options.text: Every FortiSIEM mode omits trigger events by design before incident creation.
options.feedback: Streaming and scheduled modes have different evidence capabilities.

options.label: D
options.text: The incident cap deletes trigger data when exceeded for the selected backend.
options.feedback: The incident cap limits generated incidents, not trigger-event display.

questions.stem: Which prerequisites apply to Scheduled via SQL rules in FortiSIEM 7.4?

options.label: A
options.text: Any backend and tenant mode, with unlimited incidents per run.
options.feedback: The documented mode has backend/scope restrictions and an incident cap.

options.label: B
options.text: ClickHouse and Super/Global mode, with time-only clear conditions.
options.feedback: The guide limits this mode to ClickHouse in Super/Global mode.

options.label: C
options.text: Only Elasticsearch, with streaming-style testing available before incident creation.
options.feedback: It cannot be tested like a streaming rule.

options.label: D
options.text: Any backend, but multiple clear conditions are mandatory.
options.feedback: Time is the only clear-condition option for this mode.

questions.stem: A scheduled rule with multiple subpatterns behaves unexpectedly on a non-ClickHouse backend. What should be checked?

options.label: A
options.text: Assume all scheduled rules support unlimited subpatterns on every backend.
options.feedback: Subpattern support differs by backend and mode.

options.label: B
options.text: Change event source from metrics to device inventory.
options.feedback: Changing event source does not resolve a capability limit.

options.label: C
options.text: Confirm the backend's subpattern limit and rule-mode capabilities.
options.feedback: The guide limits non-ClickHouse scheduled rules to one subpattern.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase incident severity so subpatterns execute in parallel.
options.feedback: Severity is incident metadata, not a subpattern execution control.

questions.stem: A new FortiSASE target PoP appears after migration begins. What does its initial state mean?

options.label: A
options.text: It already carries all traffic because provisioning means activation in the PoP transition.
options.feedback: The target does not carry traffic until enabled.

options.label: B
options.text: It is permanently excluded from load balancing and cannot be enabled.
options.feedback: Disabled PoPs can be enabled; they are not permanently excluded.

options.label: C
options.text: It has replaced the source and the old PoP is already deleted.
options.feedback: Source decommission happens later in the migration lifecycle.

options.label: D
options.text: It is provisioned disabled and will not accept connections until enabled.
options.feedback: Provisioning and activation are separate states in the migration flow.

questions.stem: Which FortiSASE edge deployment is most likely to need manual reconfiguration after migration?

options.label: A
options.text: An edge device that directly references the old PoP IP address.
options.feedback: Direct IP references do not automatically follow the migration.

options.label: B
options.text: An endpoint that uses the provided global FQDN during this migration.
options.feedback: The guide says FQDN-based edge deployments need no additional action.

options.label: C
options.text: A client fetching a PAC file through the global address.
options.feedback: Global PAC access normally avoids regional address changes.

options.label: D
options.text: A deployment with no reference to the source PoP for the affected endpoint.
options.feedback: No source reference means there is no old address to replace.

questions.stem: A PoP migration is left unattended. What transition is documented after 30 days?

options.label: A
options.text: The target is deleted while the source remains active indefinitely.
options.feedback: This reverses the documented transition.

options.label: B
options.text: All endpoint profiles reset to factory defaults for the affected endpoint.
options.feedback: PoP migration does not factory-reset endpoint profiles.

options.label: C
options.text: The target is automatically enabled and the source is decommissioned.
options.feedback: The guide documents automatic target activation and source decommission.

options.label: D
options.text: The target remains disabled until every client reconnects manually.
options.feedback: Manual reconnection is not the condition for the timed transition.

questions.stem: Some proxy users fail after migration while global-PAC users work. What dependency should be inspected?

options.label: A
options.text: The FortiPAM approval tier assigned to each user after target activation.
options.feedback: PAM approval does not select PAC endpoints.

options.label: B
options.text: The FortiGate SNAT source-port preservation range before source decommission for the PAC fetch path.
options.feedback: SNAT port preservation does not update PAC URLs.

options.label: C
options.text: The FortiAnalyzer fetch database rebuild state in the PoP transition during this migration.
options.feedback: Log indexing is unrelated to the endpoint's PAC fetch address.

options.label: D
options.text: Regional PAC fetch URLs and self-hosted PAC references to the old PoP.
options.feedback: Regional PAC and self-hosted references may need updating.

questions.stem: The SDN connector is connected, but new workloads do not match the SD-WAN rule. What next?

options.label: A
options.text: Change SD-WAN strategy before checking address membership for that cloud workload.
options.feedback: Path strategy is downstream of address membership.

options.label: B
options.text: Inspect the dynamic address filter and resolved IP list.
options.feedback: A connected connector can still return no matches because of filter/polling state.

options.label: C
options.text: Rotate the FortiPAM approval tier for the workload.
options.feedback: PAM approvals do not control SDN resource selection.

options.label: D
options.text: Assume connector health proves every resource matched the filter.
options.feedback: Connector health does not prove the dynamic filter matched workloads.

questions.stem: Which commands separate SDN connector health from final SD-WAN service matching?

options.label: A
options.text: Use diagnose sys session list for both connector and rule membership.
options.feedback: Session output does not show connector inventory refresh state.

options.label: B
options.text: Use ADOM revision diff and ignore the dynamic address object.
options.feedback: ADOM revisions do not show live FortiGate connector resolution.

options.label: C
options.text: Use diagnose sys sdn status, then inspect diagnose sys sdwan service.
options.feedback: The first checks connector state; the second exposes service matching.

options.label: D
options.text: Use only ping to prove the intended rule matched at path selection.
options.feedback: Ping reachability does not prove rule selection.

questions.stem: How does a cloud resource become a destination match in an SD-WAN rule?

options.label: A
options.text: The rule reads cloud tags directly without an address object.
options.feedback: The guide uses an address object to associate connector data with a rule.

options.label: B
options.text: The SLA creates IP addresses from latency measurements with the selected member.
options.feedback: An SLA measures path health, not cloud workload discovery.

options.label: C
options.text: A connector refreshes inventory into a dynamic Fabric Connector Address object.
options.feedback: The documented workflow binds connector inventory and filters to an address object.

options.label: D
options.text: The firewall policy converts every workload into a static address.
options.feedback: Dynamic connector addresses refresh rather than requiring each IP to be static.

questions.stem: The dynamic address list is correct, but traffic uses an unexpected WAN member. What next?

options.label: A
options.text: Rebuild the connector because a correct list proves it is stale.
options.feedback: A correct address list argues against a connector refresh failure.

options.label: B
options.text: Inspect rule order, strategy, and member health after confirming the match.
options.feedback: Once membership is correct, rule selection and path strategy are the next boundary.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the filter until the desired member is selected for the resolved address set.
options.feedback: Filters define destination membership, not the selected WAN member.

options.label: D
options.text: Disable all higher-priority rules without reviewing their match conditions under this service rule.
options.feedback: Blindly disabling rules can disrupt unrelated traffic and hide the match.

questions.stem: A low source port must be mapped deterministically. Which conclusion is safest?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal preservation may not apply; explicit mapping needs supported protocol and pool settings.
options.feedback: The preservation floor and explicit-mapping constraints both matter for low ports.

options.label: B
options.text: Port-preserve always retains low ports when the central rule matches under that NAT rule.
options.feedback: The documented preservation range excludes low source ports.

options.label: C
options.text: Disable reverse NAT so the peer sees the original port in the observed tuple.
options.feedback: Reverse NAT is required to map replies to the original session.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a static route to force the translated source port for this source port.
options.feedback: Routing selects a path; it does not dictate NAT port allocation.

questions.stem: After a connector filter change, a workload should move into another destination group. What must be verified first?

options.label: A
options.text: Assume SD-WAN rules never consume updated connector addresses after connector refresh for that cloud workload.
options.feedback: Dynamic connector addresses are designed to refresh external inventory.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm connector refresh completed and the dynamic object resolved the new IP set.
options.feedback: Control-plane refresh and resolved membership must be checked first.

options.label: C
options.text: Change SLA targets to the workload's previous private address at path selection.
options.feedback: SLA targets do not correct a stale address-object result.

options.label: D
options.text: Restore an ADOM revision to refresh the cloud connector automatically with the selected member.
options.feedback: ADOM restore is not the FortiGate SDN polling mechanism.
